title: The friend of Allah
hook: Ibrahim is called the friend of Allah for his wholehearted trust (4:125)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the king who argued, and the sun from the west. Your line was the sun rises where it rises. Did you let an argument go unwon? Day thirty-seven.
screen: `THE KING WHO ARGUED — THE SUN RISES WHERE IT RISES.`

segments.voice: Think about the difference between the people you know and the one or two who are your friends. Not the ones you follow, or the ones you work with. The one you'd call at three in the morning. You don't have to perform with them. You can say the plain thing: I'm scared. I don't know what to do. And they listen. Over these last days Ibrahim has watched the stars, broken the idols, faced a crowd, a fire and a king. Kings have titles. Prophets have titles too. But one name the Qur'an gives Ibrahim, the one Muslims still call him by, is the name you'd give that three-in-the-morning person.
screen: `PEOPLE YOU KNOW, AND A FRIEND.` → `THE ONE YOU'D CALL AT 3AM.` → `IBRAHIM'S NAME.`

segments.voice: Surah four, verse one twenty-five. In Pickthall's words: “Allah (Himself) chose Abraham for friend.” The Arabic word is khalil. It's a stronger word than the everyday one for a friend. Many scholars trace it to the root kh-l-l, which has to do with the gaps between things, what passes through. Scholars explain khulla as a closeness that goes all the way through, a love that fills every space in the heart and leaves no room for anything else. So when Ibrahim, watching the star set, said I love not things that set, he was clearing that space. Muslims still call him Khalilullah, the friend of God. The city of Hebron, where tradition places his tomb, is called al-Khalil in Arabic to this day. And Jews and Christians know him by the same title, friend of God, in their scriptures too. What does that friendship sound like? Listen to how Ibrahim talks about God in surah twenty-six, not like a subject to a king, but like someone describing the person closest to him. Paraphrasing: He created me, and He guides me. He feeds me and gives me to drink. And then in Pickthall's words: “And when I sicken, then He healeth me.” Food, water, getting sick. The most ordinary parts of a day. That's how a friend talks. And friendship goes both ways. Ibrahim trusted wholeheartedly: on the day of the fire, the report says, his words were simply: God is enough for us. A khalil doesn't hold back half of himself. He says the plain thing, and he listens.
screen: `CHOSE ABRAHAM FOR FRIEND.` · `KHULLA — A CLOSENESS ALL THE WAY THROUGH.` · `AL-KHALIL, THE CITY OF HEBRON.` · `WHEN I SICKEN, HE HEALS ME.` · then, large: `A FRIEND LISTENS.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. If you pray, spend one minute talking to God like a friend. No formal words. The plain thing. What today was like. What you're worried about. What you're glad of. The way Ibrahim talked about food and water and getting sick. Then spend the rest of the time just listening, in the quiet. If you don't pray, picture the person you'd call at three in the morning, and say those same plain things to them in your mind. Then listen. The bell holds the time.
Khalil. A friend of the closest kind, all the way through. The name God gives Ibrahim: Khalilullah, the friend of God.
Your line: a friend listens. Today, be that friend for one person. Ask how they really are, and then just listen, all the way through. Day thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims call Ibrahim Khalilullah, the friend of God, and many talk to God in their own words in du'a, the personal prayer that can be made any time, in any language.

original.note: Arabic: a close friend, from kh-l-l; Ibrahim is Khalilullah, the friend of God (4:125).

trapdoor: what you thought: friend of God is a nice title.
what it means: khalil — a friendship that fills the heart all the way through; God's name for Ibrahim, who trusted Him wholeheartedly.
what a scholar hears: kh-l-l, what passes between and through; khulla, above ordinary love; Hebron is al-Khalil; and the same title appears in Isaiah 41:8 and James 2:23.

notes: Pickthall 4:125 and 26:80 quoted from memory; confirm exact wording (4:125 ends '...Allah (Himself) chose Abraham for friend.').
Etymology of khalil/khulla (kh-l-l, gaps/interpenetration, takhallul): a common scholarly explanation (e.g. in lexicons and Ibn al-Qayyim). Confirm.
The index hook says 'for his wholehearted trust'; reasons commentators give for the title vary (hospitality, generosity, trust, devotion). The script ties it to trust and plain speech. Confirm.
Hebron/al-Khalil and the Cave of the Patriarchs (al-Haram al-Ibrahimi): 'where tradition places his tomb'. Handled without any political content. Confirm.
Neighbor note: Jews and Christians use the same title (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23). No comparison. Confirm.

Reviewer fixes: 'I love not things that set' (6:76) is said of the star, not the sun, so the script now says the star. The hook no longer says khalil is 'above all his other honors' (a ranking of the Qur'an's titles for Ibrahim). The khalil etymology is now framed as 'many scholars trace it'.
